result:
## Cause

The last commit, `4d99828` "Drop indexes with no recorded reads (Q3 storage review)".

Idempotency was protected by two halves, added together in `5940039`:
- the app-level check inside the transaction (`PaymentService.create`, `PaymentService.java:26-35`)
- `ux_payment_idempotency_key`, the unique index from `V2__payment_unique_index.sql`

The Q3 review dropped that index because `pg_stat_user_indexes` showed zero reads against it. It shows zero reads by design — it's a uniqueness constraint, not a lookup path, so the writes it rejects never register as scans. Removing it left only the application check, which races: on a cluster (or across two app threads), two concurrent calls with the same key can both see `existsByIdempotencyKey == false` and both insert. That's the double charge, and it's exactly the race `V2` had closed.

The application-side code is fine as it stands — the check is inside the transaction where `5940039` put it. Only the database half went missing.

## Fix

Added `src/main/resources/db/migration/V4__restore_payment_idempotency_index.sql`, recreating the index, with a comment recording why the read-count evidence was misleading so the next storage review doesn't repeat it. I did not edit `V3` — it's already applied in production, and changing it would break Flyway's checksum.

`mvn -o test` passes, though the suite is a single rounding test and doesn't exercise any of this; the migration itself needs a real Postgres to verify.

## Two things to handle before deploying

**Existing duplicates will block the index build.** Every double charge since `V3` shipped is still in the table, and `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` will fail on them. Check first:

```sql
SELECT idempotency_key, count(*), array_agg(id)
FROM payment GROUP BY idempotency_key HAVING count(*) > 1;
```

Those rows need reconciling (refund vs. void vs. delete) before the migration runs. I've deliberately left that out of the migration — which of a pair of real charges to keep, and whether money has to go back to the customer, isn't a call I should make silently inside a schema change.

**Losing races now surface as errors.** With the index back, a concurrent duplicate hits the constraint and `create` throws `DataIntegrityViolationException` instead of returning the existing payment. That's safe — it was `V2`'s behaviour too, and it fails closed rather than charging twice — but the caller sees a 500 on a request that arguably succeeded. Catching it and re-reading by key would be an improvement; it needs a retry *outside* the transaction (the current one is rollback-only once the constraint fires), so I left it out rather than bolt on something half-right. Say the word if you want it.

One unrelated observation: `Payment` has no setters for `id`, `idempotencyKey`, or `amount`, and `create` never populates them — it only sets `status`. That predates the regression (it's been that way since `be0e201`, including while the fix was working), so it isn't what's double-charging you, but if that isn't just elided scaffolding, a null `idempotency_key` would defeat the index entirely and is worth a look.
